analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil company windfall profits and curbs oil market speculation to ease record gasoline prices.
analysis.headline: The Senate placed the bill on its calendar of bills awaiting action in May 2008 and never brought it to a vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: With gasoline above $3.50 a gallon, this bill would have stripped a tax deduction from the biggest oil companies, imposed a 25% tax on their profits above their 2001–2005 average, and routed the money into a fund for cheaper and cleaner energy. It also would have made it illegal to price-gouge during a declared energy emergency, stopped new oil purchases for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, let the Justice Department sue OPEC in US courts, and forced higher down payments and more transparency in oil futures trading. It never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, workers, and small businesses paying record fuel prices, plus the renewable energy industry, which would have gained a dedicated federal fund and investment credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by record gas prices

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a 25% excise tax on the windfall profits of major integrated oil companies — those producing at least 500,000 barrels of crude a day — measured against their average inflation-adjusted profits from 2001–2005, with the tax offset by qualified investment in refineries, renewable fuel, and biofuel facilities.

It denies those same companies the domestic production tax deduction and tightens the foreign tax credit rules for foreign oil income, and puts the revenue into an Energy Independence and Security Trust Fund for easing consumer energy burdens, diversifying energy supplies, cutting greenhouse gases, and preventing price gouging.

It makes it unlawful during a presidentially declared energy emergency to sell gasoline, crude oil, petroleum products, or biofuel at an unconscionably excessive price, enforced by the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general, with civil penalties up to $5 million and criminal penalties up to $5 million and 5 years in prison.

It suspends federal purchases of oil for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve through the end of 2008 — a step aimed at keeping government demand from adding to tight supplies — until oil falls back to $75 a barrel or less.

It amends the Sherman Act (the NOPEC provision) so foreign oil cartels like OPEC can be sued in US courts for restraining trade or fixing oil prices, stripping their sovereign immunity and act-of-state protections.

It directs the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to require offshore oil trading platforms to publish trading information and position limits like US exchanges, and to substantially raise margin requirements — the cash traders must put up — on crude oil futures to curb excessive speculation.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies and their shareholders bear the new taxes; oil futures traders bear higher margin costs; foreign oil states face antitrust exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major oil companies and oil traders

drawbacks.text: A windfall profits tax can discourage domestic oil production and encourage companies to shift activity abroad; the US tried a crude oil windfall profit tax from 1980 to 1988, and studies later found it increased reliance on imported oil — a cost an honest supporter had to acknowledge.

Higher margin requirements and tighter limits on oil futures trading can reduce market liquidity, and if speculators were not the main driver of 2008's price spike, the provisions would not have lowered prices much; the bill itself ordered studies of the effects of margin changes, acknowledging the uncertainty.

The price-gouging ban applies only during a presidentially declared emergency and only to prices that are unconscionably excessive, so it would not have touched ordinary high prices driven by world market conditions.
Allowing US lawsuits against OPEC risked retaliation from oil-producing countries and diplomatic friction, a long-standing objection to the NOPEC idea.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly targeted the pocketbook pain consumers felt at the pump in 2008, and its oil-futures transparency and margin provisions addressed a real regulatory gap. The windfall tax carried a genuine design risk — it could discourage domestic production and repeat the mixed record of the 1980s version — and the price-gouging and emergency measures were narrower than the title suggests. On balance it was a consumer-focused package whose main costs would fall on large oil companies and traders, with some risk that costs were passed through to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate's calendar of bills awaiting floor action in May 2008, and it stayed there without ever coming up for a vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid introduced the Consumer-First Energy Act of 2008 on May 7, 2008, with 21 original cosponsors.
The bill was read a second time on May 8, 2008, and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 728, the list of bills awaiting floor action.
The Senate took no further action on the bill; no committee considered it and no vote was ever held before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
All 24 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's independent, and no Republican cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies, which kept their tax deductions and avoided a windfall profits tax during a year of record prices, along with oil futures traders who avoided higher margin requirements. President Bush had threatened to veto windfall tax legislation, so his position was never tested in a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies and market speculators

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar, but never brought it to the floor for a vote.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed and threatened to veto windfall profits tax legislation of this kind during the 2008 energy price debate.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Democratic oil-tax and anti-speculation package in the 2008 energy debate, blocking related Senate energy bills from reaching final passage.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 24 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent; no Republican supported the bill, and the Senate never voted on it.

industries.industry: Major integrated oil companies (producing 500,000+ barrels daily)
industries.note: The bill strips their domestic production tax deduction, tightens foreign tax credit treatment, and imposes a 25% windfall profits tax on profits above their 2001–2005 average, partially offset by credits for refinery and renewable-fuel investment. Their gain from record 2008 prices came directly out of consumers' fuel bills.

industries.industry: Oil futures speculators and offshore commodity trading platforms
industries.note: The bill requires foreign boards of trade trading US-delivered energy commodities to apply US-style transparency and position limits, and orders a substantial increase in margin requirements on crude oil trades, raising the cost of speculative positions.

The NOPEC provision makes foreign-state oil price-fixing a violation of the Sherman Act and strips sovereign immunity, exposing cartels to US antitrust enforcement for actions affecting US oil prices and supply.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and alternative fuel producers
industries.note: The new Energy Independence and Security Trust Fund would fund diversification toward secure, efficient, low-emission energy, and windfall tax liability is reduced by investment in renewable fuel and advanced biofuel facilities.
